lesson.title: One List, Two Names: Why Copying a List Isn't Automatic
lesson.summary: Because lists are mutable, writing new_list = old_list does not create a second list, it just gives the same list a second name, so changes through either name affect both.
lesson.body:
You have already learned that lists are mutable, meaning their contents can change after they are created, unlike a string or a number, which cannot be changed in place. Mutability is exactly why copying a list needs to be done on purpose. When you write alias = original for a list, Python does not build a new list and fill it with the same values. It simply makes alias point to the very same list object that original already points to. There is one list in memory now with two names attached to it.

```python
original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original
alias.append(4)
print(original)
print(alias)
```

This prints:

```
[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```

alias.append(4) looks like it only touches alias, but since alias and original are two names for the same underlying list, the change shows up no matter which name you print afterward. This is completely different from how numbers and strings behave. If original had been an immutable value, reassigning through one name would never affect the other, but mutable objects like lists do not offer that protection automatically.

To actually get a second, independent list, you have to ask for a copy explicitly. Lists provide a copy() method for exactly this purpose:

```python
original = [1, 2, 3]
copy1 = original.copy()
copy1.append(4)
print(original)
print(copy1)
```

This prints:

```
[1, 2, 3]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```

Now original and copy1 are genuinely separate list objects, so appending to one leaves the other untouched. Python offers a couple of other ways to write the same idea, list(original) and original[:] both produce an equivalent independent copy of the top level list. Which one you reach for is mostly a matter of style. What matters far more is what copy() actually promises when the list holds other lists inside it, since copying the outer list does not automatically copy everything nested inside it too, which is the exact subject of the next chapter.
